titre: Auguste Maquet, the Erased Name Behind Les Trois Mousquetaires (The Three Musketeers)
accroche: In his library, Auguste Maquet kept a copy bound in red morocco on which he had had his name engraved next to Dumas's.
contenu_vulgarise:
In his personal library, Auguste Maquet owned a copy of *Les Trois Mousquetaires* (*The Three Musketeers*) bound in red morocco, on which he had had engraved an inscription that appeared on no edition sold in bookstores: “by A. Dumas and A. Maquet.” On the cover that everyone has read since 1844, only one name appears.

## A Man in the Shadows, a Factory for Two

Maquet meets Dumas in 1838, through Gérard de Nerval. In November, he entrusts to Nerval a play he cannot get staged, *Un Soir de Carnaval* (*A Carnival Evening*); Nerval proposes it to Dumas, who reworks it following Maquet's outline and renames it *Bathilde*, without signing it. The play premieres on January 14, 1839 at the Théâtre de la Renaissance, under Maquet's name alone. Out of gratitude, Maquet then offers him a historical novel, a separate text, which he likewise cannot get published, for lack of being “a name”: Dumas reworks it in turn, and the success is immediate, *Le Chevalier d'Harmental* (*The Chevalier d'Harmental*) thus appearing as a serial in 1841. The method is found: Maquet researches, builds a plot, writes a first draft; Dumas takes up the whole, amplifies it, adds his style and his dialogue. In 1844, Maquet brings Dumas the first volumes of an adventure inspired by the *Mémoires de d'Artagnan* (*Memoirs of d'Artagnan*). Published as a serial, it becomes *Les Trois Mousquetaires*. Following, on the same model, are *Le Comte de Monte-Cristo* (*The Count of Monte Cristo*), *Vingt ans après* (*Twenty Years After*), *La Reine Margot* (*Queen Margot*), eighteen novels in all, none bearing Maquet's name.

## What the Trials Reveal

The arrangement holds as long as it stays private. In 1845, a pamphlet, *Fabrique de romans, maison Alexandre Dumas et Cie* (*Novel Factory, House of Alexandre Dumas & Co.*), makes public what the whole literary world already knew: Dumas does not work alone. A decade of lawsuits between the two men follows, Dumas defending the exclusive authorship of his novels, Maquet demanding recognition and payment. In 1857, a second trial at last settles the financial dispute: the court recognizes in Maquet neither the status of coauthor nor the right to see his name appear; it treats him as a mere creditor, like a supplier who had sold his goods, and grants him 25% of the royalties on the works written with Dumas, in exchange for his definitive renunciation of any claim to authorship.

## What This Shifts

The era has a structural need for solitary geniuses: a name that sells, a legend that can be told in one sentence. Dumas fits this need; Maquet, with his meticulous research and well-built plots, does not: he lacks the stature of the public figure that the serial-novel market demands. The historian Claude Schopp would later call him the true “fourth musketeer,” the man behind the plots. But a historian's belated recognition changes nothing about what is printed on covers still today. The mechanism, moreover, is no archaism of the 19th century: contemporary commercial literature, which sometimes pairs a famous name with cowriters who remain anonymous, unknowingly renews the same factory.

carte.punch: At home, Maquet kept a copy in which he had had his name engraved next to Dumas's.
carte.idee: Auguste Maquet coauthored eighteen novels with Alexandre Dumas, including Les Trois Mousquetaires (The Three Musketeers) and Le Comte de Monte-Cristo (The Count of Monte Cristo), without ever seeing his name on a cover sold in bookstores. In 1857, the court grants him 25% of the royalties, but denies him any right to authorship of the works.

quiz.question: What does the court decide in 1857 in the second trial between Auguste Maquet and Alexandre Dumas?
choix: It recognizes Maquet as coauthor and imposes his name on reprints
It dismisses his claim entirely: no recognition, no compensation
It treats him as a mere creditor and grants him 25% of the royalties, in return for his renunciation of any authorship claim
It transfers to Maquet the exclusive ownership of the rights to Le Comte de Monte-Cristo (The Count of Monte Cristo)
quiz.explication: The court recognizes in Maquet neither the status of coauthor nor the right to appear on covers: it equates him with a supplier who had sold his “copy” like merchandise. It grants him a share of the revenue, but no literary recognition: neither a full dismissal nor joint ownership, but a strictly financial position.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What became of the play Maquet entrusted to Nerval in November 1838?
choix: Dumas reworked it, renamed it Bathilde, and did not sign it
Nerval had it performed under his own name, without telling Maquet
It never found a theater and was not performed
Dumas turned it down, judging the plot too thin for the stage
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Dumas takes up Un Soir de Carnaval following Maquet's outline, renames it Bathilde, and does not sign it. The play premieres on January 14, 1839 at the Théâtre de la Renaissance, under Maquet's name alone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was the work divided between the two men?
choix: Dumas built the plot, Maquet wrote its dialogue
The two men wrote each chapter in strict alternation
Maquet researched and wrote a first draft, which Dumas took up
Maquet proofread novels written by Dumas alone
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Maquet did the research, built the plot and wrote a first draft; Dumas took up the whole, amplified it, and added his style and dialogue. It was neither alternation nor mere proofreading.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many novels did Maquet coauthor with Dumas, and how many bear his name?
choix: Only three novels, all signed with both names
Eighteen novels, three of which have borne both names since 1857
Eighteen novels, all later republished under both names
Eighteen novels, none of which bears his name in bookstores
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Eighteen novels, from Les Trois Mousquetaires to Le Comte de Monte-Cristo, and not a single cover sold in bookstores bearing Maquet's name. The only copy bearing both names is the one he had engraved for his library.
